To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) increasing bioenergy production in the United States and exporting wood pellets from North America to Europe increases net GHG emissions for decades or longer and (2) alternative uses of wood offer larger GHG reductions, especially when wood is substituted for fossil fuels.
increasing wood bioenergy production often increases GHG emissions and may increase climate change risks.

increasing bioenergy use in the U.S. and Canada is likely to increase net GHGs for decades, and the extent of GHG increases depends on feedstock, time horizon of the analysis, energy emissions in the supply chain, and substitution effects of bioenergy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of bioenergy production on climate change and other environmental and economic impacts.
the potential impacts of increasing biofuel production on climate, forest resources, and the economy.
the effects of increased use of forest biomass for bioenergy on the climate, the economy, and the environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

increasing bioenergy from forests and exporting pellets from North America to Europe will likely increase atmospheric concentrations of GHGs and climate warming, but the magnitude of these effects is uncertain and may depend on many factors, including the extent of land use change and other factors that are not well understood.
increasing bioenergy demand from forests is likely to increase GHGs for decades, and may increase GHGs for centuries.

the climate and environmental effects of increasing bioenergy production in North America and Europe are complex, and that the net effect on climate depends strongly on the source and fate of the biomass feedstock and the energy emissions associated with its use and substitution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
increasing biofuel production from forests can increase GHG emissions, reduce wood supply and increase prices for wood products, and affect biodiversity, soil quality, and ecosystem function.
increasing bioenergy from forests is likely to increase GHGs for decades to centuries, but that there may be circumstances in which bioenergy can reduce GHGs and provide other environmental benefits.
the use of wood as a biofuel is not a panacea for mitigating climate change, and in many circumstances it may increase GHG emissions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
increasing bioenergy from forests is not a panacea for mitigating climate change, but it can be a useful part of a comprehensive strategy for reducing GHG concentrations in the atmosphere.

the climate and other impacts of using wood from forests to produce bioenergy are complex, uncertain, and context dependent, but that there is a strong potential for increasing net emissions of GHG if bioenergy is produced from forest sources.
the net climate impacts of increasing biofuel production from forests depend on the source and scale of production, the fate of the material, and the time horizon of the analysis.
